catalog_quote: [p.322, 2.3 STRESS] The stress rules throughout the Uradhi dialects appear to be fairly uniform. The most important generalisations regarding stress are: (i) Primary stress is placed on the antepenultimate syllable, (i.e. third syllable from the end), of a word that contains only short vowels. Words of three syllables or less are therefore stressed on the initial syllable. Examples (from the Atampaya dialect): /áma/ 'person' /íku/ 'bandicoot' ... /ukúmala/ 'sweet potato' /ayparúmpiwa/ 'sparrowhawk' (ii) In the case of words containing long vowels, it is always the long vowels that receive primary stress, regardless of their position in the word. (Note that it is possible to have a word that contains two primary stresses.) The following examples (again from the Atampaya dialect) are chosen to illustrate this: ... /amá:ka/ 'message stick' ... [p.310, 1.3] ... the Cape Grenville, Margaret Bay (locally called Makkan Bay) and MacMillan River area was occupied by the wuðaði people (spelt 'Otattie' in Meston (1896:739), 'Otati' in Seligmann and Pimm (1907), 'Wo:tati' in McConnel (1939-40:55) and 'Wotadi' in Sharp (1939:257)). ... However we do have three wuðaði vocabularies, which differ lexically to a marked degree. [p.315, 1.6] There is only one phonetically accurate published source for any of these languages, and that is Hale (1964, 1976a) on the Uradhi dialect proper.

new_statements.rule_in_words: For Crowley's Uradhi dialect group (into which he places extinct Wudhadhi = Wuthathi): in words with only short vowels primary stress is antepenultimate, hence initial in words of up to three syllables; any long vowel attracts primary stress wherever it stands (two long vowels = two primary stresses). This is asserted for 'the Uradhi dialects' on Atampaya/Angkamuthi/Yadhaykenu field data; no Wuthathi form is cited and Wuthathi itself is documented only by vocabularies, so for wuth1237 this is an inference from the author's dialect grouping, not a first-hand Wuthathi observation.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described (only the possibility of two primary stresses on two long vowels is noted).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; 'appear to be fairly uniform' is the only hedge.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated on citation forms; all examples Atampaya. The only first-hand Wuthathi source (Seligmann & Pimm 1907 wordlist) is silent on stress and carries no accent marks. Glottolog 5.x does not put Wuthathi inside Uradhic (it is a separate Northeast Paman language), so applying Crowley's statement to wuth1237 depends on accepting his 1983 grouping.
new_statements.identity_note: Wuthathi (wuth1237) = Wudhadhi = 'Otati' (Seligmann & Pimm 1907), 'Otattie' (Meston 1896), 'Wo:tati' (McConnel 1939-40), 'Wotadi' (Sharp 1939); extinct. Crowley 1983 treats Wudhadhi (with neighbouring Mutyanthi) as a south-eastern dialect of his 'Uradhi' language, whose described dialects are Atampaya (atam1239), Angkamuthi and Yadhaykenu (yadh1237; Glottolog family node yadh1238; retired urad1239). Glottolog 5.x instead lists Wuthathi as a separate language under Northeast Paman (nort3278), outside Uradhic (urad1238). The quoted stress statement is Crowley's for the Uradhi dialect group and is already keyed in the 2026-09-12 catalog under atam1239 (same page, p.322); attaching it to wuth1237 would duplicate that lineage and rests on no Wuthathi data.

readall_conflicts: Crowley 1983 (§2.3, p.322; existing statement) describes synchronic stress in the Uradhi dialects as antepenultimate in all-short-vowel words (initial in words of up to three syllables) with long vowels always taking primary stress, i.e. weight-sensitive. Hale 1964 (p.256) says that in the Northern Paman development primary stress, 'a strictly phonetic feature', shifted from the initial to the second syllable of Paman stems, which is a different placement and treats stress as non-contrastive. The disagreement is partly one of level: Hale's is a diachronic claim about the pre-reduction stage of the whole Northern Paman group, Crowley's a synchronic description of modern Uradhi dialects; for languages that dropped the initial syllable the two are compatible, but for the Uradhi group (which retained *V1, Hale p.260) they are not, and Hale gives no modern-language examples with stress marked that would settle it. Neither source has Wudhadhi data: Crowley knew Wudhadhi only from vocabularies, Hale only as the name Wɔ:tati in McConnel's ethnography.
